subjects.introduction: A dungeon beneath Ṭihrán, a mountain fortress with two guards and four dogs, a barracks in ‘Akká where the first night passed without water: in such places the Báb, Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá spent the years that gave the world a new Faith. Bahá’u’lláh does not hide the cost. He says that the cruelties of His oppressors bowed Him down and turned His hair white [1], and He gave ‘Akká the name of the Most Great Prison, a name He had refused to the pit of His chains in Ṭihrán [2]. Yet the same pen calls a pauper’s mat of straw an eternal throne, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls His cage a heavenly rose garden and asks His friends to pray that His tribulations be increased. The question opened here is not whether suffering can be avoided but what it can be made to carry: the freedom of other souls, the proof that a love is real. From this threshold the way leads on through the long banishments, the tests and trials every believer meets, and the consolation of bearing them with a steadfast heart.

order.why: These readings survey the whole span of the sufferings. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and His reported talks recount the chains and the threat of the sword in Persia, the banishment to Baghdád, Constantinople and Adrianople, and the confinement in ‘Akká, and say that Bahá’u’lláh found not a moment’s rest nor drew a tranquil breath. One passage contrasts the nest of every bird with the Manifestation who had no resting place; another says that His pauper’s mat of straw was to Him an eternal throne of glory. The talks name purposes for this suffering: the betterment of the world, the oneness of humanity and love among the nations. Why do these summaries return so often to rest denied? What does it mean to call such a life a gift to the world?

In Persia, He was imprisoned and bound in chains, was under constant threat of the sword, and was made to suffer grievous blows. He was then banished from Persia to Baghdad and lived as an exile in that land. He later became captive in the Prison of 'Akka and, while confined and in chains, promulgated His Cause and raised the banner of the oneness of humankind.

These readings turn to the Báb. A Traveller’s Narrative records how the learned doctors agreed on His suppression, how He was held forty days in Tabríz and nine months in the castle of Máh-Kú, and how the doctors met and wrote their verdict; the same account carries Bahá’u’lláh’s words on the coming move to ‘Akká. In His own writings the Báb says that He was patient until judged without justice to imprisonment in the depths of the mountain, describes a fortress with two guards and four dogs, finds the mountain pleasant because it accords with the Beloved’s good-pleasure, and thanks God for turning the prison into a garden of Paradise. Elsewhere He asks what greater honour there could be than martyrdom. How does the Báb speak of His prisons? What links His longing for sacrifice to the accounts of His martyrdom?
shortened: Although He remained forty days in the city of Tabriz the learned doctors did not condescend to approach Him and did not deem it right to meet Him. Then they sent Him off to the Castle of Maku, and for nine months lodged Him in the inaccessible castle which is situated on the summit of that lofty mountain.

"We are about to shift from this most remote place of banishment unto the prison of 'Akka. And, according to what they say, it is assuredly the most desolate of the cities of the world, the most unsightly of them in appearance, the most detestable in climate, and the foulest in water; it is as though it were the metropolis of the owl; there is not heard from its regions aught save the sound of its hooting. And in it they intend to imprison the Servant, and to shut in Our faces the doors of leniency and take away from Us the good things of the life of the world during what remaineth of Our days.

order.why: These readings stay in Ṭihrán. Bahá’u’lláh recalls being hurried along by a troop of executioners while a man on horseback snatched off His hat, four months in a place foul beyond comparison, feet in stocks and the most galling of chains, companions who were mostly thieves and highwaymen, two days without food, thumbs bound behind the back and an executioner who brought Him tea. Accounts by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and others add the walk bareheaded and barefoot from Níyávarán, the chain that bound Him to five other Bábís, an attempt to poison Him, and a son’s glimpse of his Father at the noon airing of the prisoners. One passage recalls nights when He kissed the chains for love of God. What do these first-hand details add to the summaries? How can the same dungeon be both darkness and the place where chains were kissed?
shortened: A brutal man, accompanying Us on horseback, snatched off Our hat, whilst We were being hurried along by a troop of executioners and officials. We were consigned for four months to a place foul beyond comparison. As to the dungeon in which this Wronged One and others similarly wronged were confined, a dark and narrow pit were preferable.

The dungeon was wrapped in thick darkness, and Our fellow prisoners numbered nearly a hundred and fifty souls: thieves, assassins and highwaymen. Though crowded, it had no other outlet than the passage by which We entered. No pen can depict that place, nor any tongue describe its loathsome smell.

order.why: These readings follow the banishments. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá counts four times that Bahá’u’lláh was rendered homeless, from Ṭihrán to Baghdád, Constantinople, Adrianople and ‘Akká. Reported talks recall a winter so cold that water froze and broke its jars, a mother shaking flour into her child’s hand after the plunder of their house in Ṭihrán, and the worn coat of Bahá’u’lláh on His return from Sulaymáníyyih. Tablets record the twelve days in the Garden of Riḍván, the soldiers surrounding the house in Adrianople, the auction of the household’s goods, a companion who cut his throat and another who cast himself into the sea, and the captivity of His loved ones in ‘Iráq, carried to Mosul after they had been commanded not to kill even if they were killed. How do these accounts join outward loss to inward constancy? What did the command not to kill ask of the believers?
shortened: Know thou, O servant, that one day, upon awakening, We found the beloved of God at the mercy of Our adversaries. Sentinels were posted at every gate and no one was permitted to enter or leave. Indeed, they perpetrated a sore injustice, for the loved ones of God and His kindred were left on the first night without food. Such was the fate of those for whose sake the world and all that is therein have been created.

order.why: These readings enter the Most Great Prison. Bahá’u’lláh records the first night in the barracks without food or drink, companions lying sick, three months without a bath, no barber admitted without guards, and seventy souls imprisoned with Him; twenty women entered the prison out of love. In one prayer He shows God His son blood-stained before Him. Reported talks describe the foul water and air, guards too sick to give water, a damp room with grass on its walls, thirteen people in one room, a carpet sold to bury two companions, and nine years without the sight of a green leaf. Yet the same readings speak of commemorating the Feast and the Riḍván Festival in the Prison and of joy beyond words in the direst straits. How do the readings hold these together? What is gained by naming this place the Most Great Prison?
shortened: Upon our arrival, we were surrounded by guards and confined together, men and women, young and old alike, in the army barracks.  The first night all were deprived of either food or drink, for the sentries were guarding the gate of the barracks and permitted no one to leave.  No one gave a thought to the plight of these wronged ones.  They even begged for water, and were refused.
Most of Our companions now lie sick in this prison, and none knoweth what befell Us, except God, the Almighty, the All-Knowing.

These readings let Bahá’u’lláh speak of the weight of what befell Him. Twenty years, He tells the kings, have passed with the agony of a fresh tribulation each day; heaven, earth and mountains could not bear a single atom of it; were the sun acquainted with His sorrows it would rise no more. A thousand seas of ink would not suffice to record them, His black hair has turned white, the story of Ḥusayn has been repeated in His prison, and He hears even nature lamenting in ‘Akká. Several passages say that His deepest grief comes not from chains or enemies but from those who claim to love Him: the brother He had nurtured, who was the first to seek His blood, and loved ones who follow their own desires. Why might betrayal weigh more than imprisonment? Why does He say that He has concealed His woes?
shortened: Blessed is He Who hath sent down upon His Servant such tribulations as have melted the hearts of them that dwell within the Tabernacle of eternity and the souls of those who have drawn nigh unto their Lord.  Blessed is He Who hath showered upon His Servant, from the clouds of His decree, the darts of affliction, and Who beholdeth Me enduring them with patience and fortitude.  Blessed is He Who hath ordained for His Servant that which He hath destined for no other soul.

Twenty years, He tells the kings, have passed with the agony of a fresh tribulation each day; heaven, earth and mountains could not bear a single atom of it; were the sun acquainted with His sorrows it would rise no more. A thousand seas of ink would not suffice to record them, His black hair has turned white, the story of Ḥusayn has been repeated in His prison, and He hears even nature lamenting in ‘Akká. Several passages say that His deepest grief comes not from chains or enemies but from those who claim to love Him: the brother He had nurtured, who was the first to seek His blood, and loved ones who follow their own desires. Why might betrayal weigh more than imprisonment? Why does He say that He has concealed His woes?
shortened: Not a single night in Mine earthly life did I find rest; not a single day was I granted repose.

Every morn, as I arose from My bed, a fresh affliction awaited Me; and every eve, as I repaired to the solitude of My chamber, a sore trial was in store. In the succession of My woes there was no reprieve, and in the onslaught of My sorrows there was no respite.

These readings set the sufferings of this Day within the history of every Messenger. The Kitáb-i-Íqán asks why, despite the expectation of men and the signs recorded in the sacred books, every Prophet has met with oppression, and points to those who occupied the seats of authority and learning. Bahá’u’lláh asks what proof the Jewish doctors adduced against Christ and recounts the judgment of Annas. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes Abraham forsaking His native land with scarcely anyone beside Him but Lot, the disciples of Christ imprisoned and martyred, and Christ under the crown of thorns beholding the crowns of kings bowing before it. Reported talks take up why Christ prayed that the cup might pass, and note that Christ was opposed by the Jews while this Manifestation was opposed by the whole world. What pattern do these readings trace? How does knowing it change what a believer expects?
shortened: Why then is it that despite the expectation of men in their quest of the Manifestations of Holiness, and in spite of the signs recorded in the sacred books, such acts of violence, of oppression and cruelty, should have been perpetrated in every age and cycle against all the Prophets and chosen Ones of God? Even as He hath revealed: "As oft as an Apostle cometh unto you with that which your souls desire not, ye swell with pride, accusing some of being impostors and slaying others."
What unspeakable cruelties they that have occupied the seats of authority and learning have inflicted upon the true Monarchs of the world, those Gems of divine virtue!

Reported talks take up why Christ prayed that the cup might pass, and note that Christ was opposed by the Jews while this Manifestation was opposed by the whole world. What pattern do these readings trace? How does knowing it change what a believer expects?

These readings give a purpose to the sufferings. Bahá’u’lláh writes that His body has borne imprisonment that the souls of others may be released from bondage and that He consented to be abased that they might be exalted; He chose imprisonment for Himself and freedom for His servants, and gives thanks for being imprisoned for the emancipation of the worlds. A prayer asks how, had He not been established in the Most Great Prison, the Cause could have spread abroad. Tribulation is called the oil for His Lamp and a help to this Revelation, and a reported talk says that under the chains He unfurled the flag of the oneness of humanity. Other passages say that those who imagine they can extinguish the light of God have grievously erred. What does it mean that one person’s suffering frees others? How is imprisonment turned into proclamation?
shortened: I have summoned the people unto none save God, thy Lord and the Lord of the worlds, and have endured for love of Him such afflictions as the eye of creation hath never beheld.

Whensoever the clouds of tribulation have rained down the darts of affliction in the path of God, the Lord of all names, I have hastened to meet them, as every fair-minded and discerning soul shall attest.  How many the nights which found the beasts of the field resting in their lairs, and the birds of the air lying in their nests, while this Youth languished in chains and fetters with none to aid or succour Him!

A prayer asks how, had He not been established in the Most Great Prison, the Cause could have spread abroad. Tribulation is called the oil for His Lamp and a help to this Revelation, and a reported talk says that under the chains He unfurled the flag of the oneness of humanity. Other passages say that those who imagine they can extinguish the light of God have grievously erred. What does it mean that one person’s suffering frees others? How is imprisonment turned into proclamation?
shortened: Baha'u'llah suffered forty years as a prisoner and exile in order that the Kingdom of love might be established in the East and West. He has made it possible for us to meet here in love and unity. Because He suffered imprisonment, we are free to proclaim the oneness of the world of humanity for which He stood so long and faithfully. He was chained in dungeons, He was without food, His companions were thieves and criminals, He was subjected to every kind of abuse and infliction, but throughout it all He never ceased to proclaim the reality of the Word of God and the oneness of humanity.

These readings speak of joy in tribulation. Bahá’u’lláh calls the pit His house and the prison His palace, anxiety His gladness and the prison His paradise, and says that the Youth has grown intimate with tribulations as infants with their mothers’ breasts. A prayer gives thanks that God has chosen the Prison as the throne of His kingdom; another exclaims how sweet is the injury suffered in His love; another wishes that life could be prolonged so as to be afflicted anew each day. He recalls a time without food, drink or a place to rest that was spent in a joy no worldly joy could equal, and a reported talk says that even in prison He was like a king enthroned. Is this joy a denial of suffering or a way through it? Why might the homeland of those near to God be the prison?
shortened: Know thou, moreover, that We have been cast into an afflictive Prison, and are encompassed with the hosts of tyranny, as a result of what the hands of the infidels have wrought. Such is the gladness, however, which the Youth hath tasted that no earthly joy can compare unto it. By God! The harm He suffereth at the hands of the oppressor can never grieve His heart, nor can He be saddened by the ascendancy of such as have repudiated His truth.

These readings belong to ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, a prisoner for forty years. He bids the friends rejoice in His bondage, which sows the seeds of freedom, calls the prison a palace and the cage a heavenly rose garden, and declines a release that notables could have procured because the citadel was the prison of the Abhá Beauty. He asks those who would pray for Him to pray that His tribulation be increased. Other passages show the cost: no one went to bed expecting to see the morrow, every loaf was cut open by the guard, enemies waited to cast Him into the sea or banish Him to Fezzan, and a prison was set within the prison. When the chains passed from His neck to ‘Abdu’l-Ḥamíd’s, He journeyed to the West. How did ‘Abdu’l-Bahá turn confinement into service? What does His refusal of release teach?
shortened: Baha'u'llah passed forty years of His life in prison and exile in order that He might upraise the banner of the oneness of the world of men.
He was under the dominion of Abdu'l-Hamid. I, too, was in the prison of Abdu'l-Hamid until the Committee of Union and Progress hoisted the standard of liberty and my fetters were removed.

He bids the friends rejoice in His bondage, which sows the seeds of freedom, calls the prison a palace and the cage a heavenly rose garden, and declines a release that notables could have procured because the citadel was the prison of the Abhá Beauty. He asks those who would pray for Him to pray that His tribulation be increased. Other passages show the cost: no one went to bed expecting to see the morrow, every loaf was cut open by the guard, enemies waited to cast Him into the sea or banish Him to Fezzan, and a prison was set within the prison. When the chains passed from His neck to ‘Abdu’l-Ḥamíd’s, He journeyed to the West. How did ‘Abdu’l-Bahá turn confinement into service? What does His refusal of release teach?
shortened: I myself was in prison forty years -- one year alone would have been impossible to bear -- nobody survived that imprisonment more than a year! But, thank God, during all those forty years I was supremely happy! Every day, on waking, it was like hearing good tidings, and every night infinite joy was mine. Spirituality was my comfort, and turning to God was my greatest joy.

shortened: To have been lodged in this faraway prison is for me exceeding joy. By the life of Baha! This prison is my supernal paradise; it is my cherished goal, the comfort of my bosom, the bliss of my heart; it is my refuge, my shelter, my asylum, my safe haven, and within it do I exult amid the hosts of heaven and the Company on high.

'Abdu'l-Baha fell under severe surveillance from all directions, to the point where breath became constricted and souls could no longer bear to wait.

Therefore, how can I, Who follow in His footsteps, be perturbed by the threat of injury, captivity or death?"

These readings turn to the believers. Bahá’u’lláh blesses those who have been imprisoned for His sake, tells a prisoner that He too is imprisoned by the decree of God, calls the humiliation of the loved ones the pride and glory of all temporal honour, and praises God for making the tyranny of the unjust a means whereby true lovers draw nigh. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that troubles come so that the friends may share in His tribulations, and rebukes tears over a few days of hardship borne in the footsteps of the Blessed Beauty. The readings recall believers who rushed dancing to the field of sacrifice and women paraded through the bazaars. One Tablet bids those who call themselves His lovers be ashamed of conduct unworthy of His sufferings, and prayers ask that hearts be made as strong as brass. How should a believer regard personal hardship in this light? What does it mean to share in another’s tribulation?

The linked readings close with prayers revealed in and about the prison. Many are Bahá’u’lláh’s own: Thou beholdest me in the clutches of my oppressors; Thou seest me sitting under a sword hanging on a thread; How many the nights, O my Best-Beloved, during which I lay a captive. They describe a place within whose walls no voice is heard except the echo, a prison-house behind the seas and the mountains, and a Lamp that no tempest has put out. Some give thanks for being made a target for the darts of the adversaries; one asks for the crown of martyrdom; others plead for the loved ones. One bears witness that the eye of creation has never gazed upon one wronged like Him. How do these prayers move between complaint and thanksgiving? What might a reader learn by praying them?
shortened: I bear witness that the eye of creation hath never gazed upon one wronged like Thee. Thou wast immersed all the days of Thy life beneath an ocean of tribulations. At one time Thou wast in chains and fetters; at another Thou wast threatened by the sword of Thine enemies.

shortened: Praise be to Thee, O Lord My God, for the wondrous revelations of Thy inscrutable decree and the manifold woes and trials Thou hast destined for Myself. At one time Thou didst deliver Me into the hands of Nimrod; at another Thou hast allowed Pharaoh's rod to persecute Me. Thou, alone, canst estimate, through Thine all-encompassing knowledge and the operation of Thy Will, the incalculable afflictions I have suffered at their hands. Again Thou didst cast Me into the prison-cell of the ungodly, for no reason except that I was moved to whisper into the ears of the well-favored denizens of Thy Kingdom an intimation of the vision with which Thou hadst, through Thy knowledge, inspired Me, and revealed to Me its meaning through the potency of Thy might. And again Thou didst decree that I be beheaded by the sword of the infidel. Again I was crucified for having unveiled to men's eyes the hidden gems of Thy glorious unity, for having revealed to them the wondrous signs of Thy sovereign and everlasting power.

Some give thanks for being made a target for the darts of the adversaries; one asks for the crown of martyrdom; others plead for the loved ones. One bears witness that the eye of creation has never gazed upon one wronged like Him. How do these prayers move between complaint and thanksgiving? What might a reader learn by praying them?

Though the sword be ready to fall on my head, I call Thy loved ones with such a calling that the hearts are carried away towards the horizon of Thy majesty and grandeur.

In this authorized passage Bahá’u’lláh explains that on arriving at ‘Akká He chose to name it the Most Great Prison, though He had refused that name to Ṭihrán, where He had been in chains and fetters, and asks those endued with understanding to ponder it. questions: Why do these readings so often say that the Manifestation found no rest? Compare the summaries of a life without a tranquil breath with the first-hand details of the dungeon in Ṭihrán, the house surrounded in Adrianople and the barracks of ‘Akká. What does each kind of account show that the other cannot?

How can a prison be called a palace, a paradise or a rose garden? Read the passages of the Báb, Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that speak this way beside those describing foul air, hunger and chains. Is the change in the place, in the prisoner or in the purpose?

Bahá’u’lláh writes that His body bore imprisonment that the souls of others might be released from bondage. What kinds of freedom do the readings connect with His imprisonment, and how do they link suffering with the proclamation of the Cause from the prison?
Several passages say that His deepest grief came not from enemies but from those who claimed to love Him. Why might this be so, and what does it ask of those who call themselves His lovers?

What pattern do the readings trace in the opposition faced by Abraham, Moses, Christ, Muhammad, the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh? Who led the opposition in each case, and why do the readings say that it arose despite long expectation?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the friends to share in His tribulations and to pray that His own be increased, while other prayers ask that the believers be kept steadfast and protected. How do the readings hold together the longing for tribulation and the prayer for relief and strength?
